analysis.one_liner: Caps the interest rate on consumer credit, including credit cards, at 15 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 2011-2012 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a 15 percent annual rate cap into federal law for all consumer credit, including every finance charge and fee, so lenders could not dodge it by renaming charges. A lender who overcharged would have to give back all the interest, and borrowers could sue to recover it. The Federal Reserve could raise the cap temporarily if market rates rose enough to threaten lenders' finances, and credit unions were exempt. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who pay high rates on credit cards and other consumer loans, especially people carrying balances at rates of 20 to 30 percent. The bill also let borrowers who were overcharged recover all the interest they had paid, going back two years.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any consumer extension of credit at 15 percent, counting all finance charges, and bars lenders from using non-finance-charge fees to evade the cap — fees beyond that could not exceed the finance charges allowed. [S3]

Gives borrowers a remedy: a lender who knowingly charges above the cap forfeits all the interest on the loan, and a borrower can sue within two years to recover every interest charge and fee paid. [S3]

Creates a safety valve so credit stays available: the Federal Reserve could raise the ceiling above 15 percent for periods up to 18 months if money-market rates had risen and prevailing rates threatened lenders' liquidity, capital, earnings, and growth. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, payday lenders, and other consumer lenders, who would lose the difference between rates above 15 percent and the cap, and high-risk borrowers who might find less credit offered to them at that price.

drawbacks.text: A hard 15 percent cap would cut off most credit to higher-risk borrowers, who today are priced at rates above that level; lenders facing a binding cap generally reduce lending rather than extend unprofitable loans. [S3]

The cap is strict enough that the Fed's escape clause only applies when lender finances — liquidity, capital, earnings, and growth — are deteriorating, which limits flexibility if rates rise for other reasons. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households carrying balances near 30 percent, the cap is a large, direct savings, and the refund-and-forfeiture provisions give it teeth that prior usury bills lacked. The real cost falls on borrowers with weak credit histories, who under a 15 percent ceiling may be offered no credit at all rather than expensive credit — a serious trade-off, but one the bill accepted deliberately.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, later sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2013. [S5]

narrative.text: Introduced January 19, 2011 by Rep. Maurice Hinchey with seven Democratic cosponsors. [S3]
Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day. [S5]
Referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit on March 23, 2011, where no further action was recorded. [S5]
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer lenders kept charging rates above 15 percent, and households carrying high-interest balances kept paying them, because the bill never left committee.

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap consumer credit rates at 15 percent. [S3]

for.name: Seven House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Tierney, Cohen, Filner, Miller, Woolsey, Grijalva, Jackson)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced. [S3]

against.name: Rep. Spencer Bachus
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the two years it sat on the committee's agenda.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-run Financial Services Committee never acted on the bill; there were no roll-call votes.

industries.note: A 15 percent all-in cap on consumer credit would eliminate most of the interest revenue on credit card balances, which commonly run 20-30 percent. Issuers generally opposed national rate caps. [S3]
A 15 percent cap, inclusive of all fees, would end the short-term, high-fee lending model, whose effective annual rates run in the hundreds of percent. [S3]
The cap expressly exempts insured credit unions, letting them lend at their existing rates while banks face the ceiling — a competitive advantage for not-for-profit member lenders. [S3]
